We have mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100) as base peak. Likely molecular ion [M+H]+? Usually mass spec gives m/z of molecular ion. 179.0946 corresponds to formula? Let's compute possible formula. Use typical atomic masses: C=12.0000, H=1.007825, N=14.00307, O=15.99491. Let's guess C10H13NO2: mass = 10*12=120 +13*1.007825=13.1017 +14.00307=14.00307 +2*15.99491=31.9898 total = 179.09457. Yes matches. So molecular formula C10H13NO2. Good.

We have proton NMR: signals: 2.58 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 2.84 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 3.81 (s, 3H), aromatic: 7.17 (ddd, 2H), 7.93 (ddd, 2H). So aromatic ring with 4 aromatic protons (para-disubstituted). Two ethylene CH2 groups (CH2-CH2) adjacent to carbonyl? The 2.58 and 2.84 both triplets 2H each, typical for -CH2-CH2- chain. 3.81 s 3H likely methoxy OCH3 attached to aromatic. So structure: para-methoxy phenyl attached to something with -CH2-CH2-CO-NH? Actually we have amide (C=O N). The formula includes one N, two O (one carbonyl, one methoxy). So likely p-methoxy phenyl attached to CH2-CH2-CO-NH (or CO-NH-CH2-CH2-Ph?). Let's examine chemical shifts: CH2 next to carbonyl (CH2-CO) appears around 2.3-2.5. CH2 next to aromatic appears around 2.7-3.0. Here we have 2.58 and 2.84 both triplets, J 7.4 indicates adjacent CH2. So chain -CH2-CH2- between carbonyl and aromatic? If carbonyl attached to N (amide) then CH2 next to carbonyl is alpha to carbonyl (CH2-CO) ~2.3. CH2 next to aromatic ~2.7-3.0. So plausible: OCH3-Ph-CH2-CH2-CO-NH (i.e., p-methoxy phenylpropionamide? Actually that's phenethyl amide). Let's compute formula for CO-NH-CH2-CH2-Ph-OCH3. Count: phenyl (C6H4) because para substituents two: OCH3 and CH2CH2CONH. OCH3 adds OCH3 (CH3O) = C1H3O1. Chain: CH2-CH2-CO-NH adds C3H6NO? Wait CH2-CH2-CO (C3H4O) plus NH (N H). Actually CH2-CH2-CO-NH: atoms: C (CH2)2 = C2H4, carbonyl carbon = C1O1, NH = N1H1. So total C3H5NO? Let's sum: CH2-CH2-CO-NH: C3 (2+1), H5 (4+1), N1, O1. Add phenyl C6H4 (since two substituents replace two H). So C9H9? Wait phenyl C6H4 plus substituents: OCH3 adds C1H3O1, chain adds C3H5NO. Total C6+1+3=10 C. H: phenyl 4 +3 +5 =12? plus maybe NH hydrogen counted already in chain (5 includes NH). So total H = 4+3+5 =12. But formula we need C10H13NO2. We have H12, need H13. Maybe there is an extra hydrogen on nitrogen? Already counted. Actually chain CH2-CH2-CO-NH: the NH has one H. So H count correct. But we need one more H, maybe the aromatic ring is not para but meta? But OCH3 adds 3 H, chain adds 5, phenyl 4 =12. So missing one H. Could be that the amide is N-methyl? But formula only one N, two O. N-methyl would add CH3 and remove NH H, still same H count? N-methyl would add C1H3, remove H from NH, net +C1H2, increasing H by 2, not correct.

Alternatively maybe the chain is -CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 (primary amide). That would add NH2 (N1H2) instead of NH (N1H1). Then H count +1. Let's compute: CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: C3H5NO? Actually CH2-CH2 = C2H4, carbonyl C1O1, NH2 adds N1H2. Total C3H6NO? Wait H: 4+2 =6. So chain H6. Phenyl H4, OCH3 H3 => total H13. Yes matches C10H13NO2. So structure: p-methoxy phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 (para-methoxy phenethyl amide). That is 4-(methoxy)phenethylamide? Actually phenethyl amide: 4-methoxyphenethylamide (p-anisic acid amide?). Wait anisic acid is p-methoxybenzoic acid (COOH attached directly to ring). Here we have ethyl amide attached to ring via CH2CH2. So name: 4-methoxyphenethylamide.

SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N? Let's check: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N. This is methoxy phenyl attached to CH2-CH2-CO-NH. Yes matches. Validate earlier we validated that SMILES and it's true. Let's compute formula: C? Count: COc1ccc(cc1) = anisole ring: C7H7O? Actually anisole C7H8O? Wait anisole (methoxybenzene) formula C7H8O. But we have additional CH2CH2CONH: C3H6NO? Actually CH2CH2C(=O)N adds C3H6NO. Sum C10H14NO? Wait anisole C7H8O, plus C3H6NO = C10H14NO2? Let's compute: anisole C7H8O (C7 H8 O1). Add chain C3 H6 N1 O1 => total C10 H14 N1 O2. That's C10H14NO2, not C10H13NO2. But our SMILES COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N includes anisole ring with OCH3 (C1H3O) plus phenyl C6H4 (since two substituents). So total C7H7O? Wait anisole ring with OCH3 attached to ring: OCH3 attached to aromatic carbon, the aromatic carbon loses H. So phenyl C6H4 plus OCH3 C1H3O => C7H7O. Yes anisole formula C7H8O? Actually anisole is C7H8O (C6H5-O-CH3). That's C7H8O. Wait C6H5 + CH3O = C7H8O. Yes C7H8O. But our ring has also CH2CH2CONH attached, replacing another H, so phenyl becomes C6H3 (since two substituents). So base phenyl C6H3. Add OCH3 C1H3O, add chain C3H6NO. Total C10 H12? Let's compute: C6H3 + C1H3 + C3H6 = C10 H12. O from OCH3 + O from carbonyl = O2. N1. So C10H12NO2. But we need H13. Something off.

Let's compute more systematically: SMILES COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N.

Breakdown: aromatic ring c1ccc(cc1) is C6H4 (since two substituents). The OCH3 attached: CO- means OCH3 attached to aromatic carbon: OCH3 adds C1H3O1. The side chain: CC(=O)N is -CH2- C(=O)N? Actually "CC(=O)N" after aromatic means -CH2- C(=O)N (i.e., ethyl amide). The first C is CH2 attached to ring, second C is carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to N. So side chain atoms: CH2 (C1H2), carbonyl carbon (C1O1), N (N1H2? Actually amide N has two H? In SMILES "N" default is NH2? In "C(=O)N" the N has one H (since valence 3). So N has one H. So side chain hydrogens: CH2 (2 H) + N (1 H) = 3 H. Also there is maybe another CH2? Wait "CC(=O)N": first C is CH2 attached to ring, second C is carbonyl carbon (no H). So only one CH2, not two. So chain is phenyl-CH2-CO-NH2? Actually carbonyl carbon attached to N, N has one H (NH). But SMILES "N" default is NH2? In amide, carbonyl carbon has double bond O, single bond N, N has one H (since valence 3). So N has one H. So side chain is -CH2-CO-NH. That's only one CH2, not two. But our NMR shows two CH2 triplets, indicating two CH2 groups. So SMILES should be phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. That would be "COc1ccc(cc1)CCCN"? Wait need carbonyl: phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: SMILES "COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)N"? That is phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2? Actually "CC(=O)N" after aromatic includes two carbons: first C is CH2 attached to ring, second C is carbonyl carbon. That's only one CH2. To have two CH2, need "CCC(=O)N": phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N. Let's test formula: phenyl C6H3, OCH3 C1H3O, chain C3H6NO? chain: CH2-CH2-CO-NH2: CH2 (2H) + CH2 (2H) + carbonyl C (0H) + N (2H) = H6. So total H: phenyl 3 + OCH3 3 + chain 6 =12? Wait phenyl C6H3 has 3 H. So total H =3+3+6=12. But formula needed H13. Maybe N has one H not two? Actually amide NH2 has two H? In primary amide, carbonyl C attached to NH2 (two H). So N has two H. So chain H: CH2 (2) + CH2 (2) + N (2) =6. Yes. So total H =3+3+6=12. Still 12. Something off: maybe phenyl has 4 H (if only one substituent OCH3 and chain attached at para? Actually we have two substituents para to each other, so phenyl C6H4 (two substituents replace two H). So phenyl H =4. Wait earlier we said C6H3 but that's for two substituents? Actually benzene C6H6. Two substituents replace two H, leaving C6H4. Yes phenyl H=4. So phenyl H=4. Then OCH3 adds 3 H, chain adds 6 H =13. Good! So formula C10H13NO2 matches.

Thus SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)N. Let's validate.
